item.title: Pogacar 'happy to be alive' after 'scary' crash
item.description: Five-time Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar says he is "just happy to be alive", two months after suffering three fractured vertebrae in a crash.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Five-time Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar says he is "just happy to be alive", two months after suffering three fractured vertebrae in a crash.

The 28-year-old Slovenian was ruled out for the season after crashing during the Vuelta a Espana in August.

Pogacar required surgery on a broken collarbone and was initially diagnosed with a fracture in his neck, but further scans in his home country revealed more injuries.

"I knew I had a C7 fracture, but then we saw I had two more broken vertebrae, the T1 and T2," Pogacar told The Athletic, external.

"At that moment, I was happy I didn't do the European Championships, which had been my initial goal. When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I'm just happy to be alive actually, or just to be standing."

Pogacar also suffered concussion during the crash, which left him struggling with dizziness, nausea and poor co-ordination in the weeks afterwards.

He said the extent of the concussion meant he was unable to shower by himself.

"I had to be showered with the help of the team doctor. I could not shower. I was getting dizzy as soon as I stood or when I put my head down," Pogacar added.

"I was just completely out of it and it was so tough."

When he came off his bike, Pogacar was aiming to complete the set of Grand Tour titles by adding the Vuelta to his single Giro d'Italia victory and five Tour de France wins.

His injuries meant he was unable to defend his rainbow jersey at the World Championships in Montreal last month.

Pogacar said the first few weeks of recovery were difficult and he was "mentally not OK" and "not a fun person to be around".

He said his mood improved once he resumed rehabilitation and indoor training.

"When I started to get on the home trainer, to go to physio every day, then I started to feel better, also in the head. But it was a day-to-day fight," he said.

"I don't have discomfort any more. I have to be careful not to crash on the bike, or do some heavy lifting with my left arm or with my neck. But I can do basically everything normal now."

Pogacar's team UAE Team Emirates-XRG said the decision not to race again until 2027 would allow him to return to full health "without placing a timeline on his return to competition".

Pogacar is aiming to return next year, but will do so with a more cautious mindset.

"If I crash again on the bike now, it can be very problematic. Everybody says that I was lucky, and you're always lucky after a crash where you can walk away and you're fine," said Pogacar.

"You see it's pretty serious and not to joke around. It's a bit scary, to be honest, to think about it."

item.title: Kane beat Mbappe to Ballon d'Or by just 28 points
item.description: Voting figures show Harry Kane beat second-placed Kylian Mbappe to the men's Ballon d'Or by one of the tightest winning margins in the award's history.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Harry Kane beat second-placed Kylian Mbappe to the men's Ballon d'Or by just 28 points - one of the smallest winning margins in the award's history.

Organisers released voting numbers on Saturday, showing that England captain Kane was awarded 1,055 points, compared with 1,027 for Real Madrid's France forward Mbappe.

Bayern Munich striker Kane became the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001, while France talisman Mbappe also claimed his best finish, ending up well clear of Spain forward Lamine Yamal, who was third with 881 points.

It was the smallest winning margin since Argentina great Lionel Messi beat Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk by seven points in 2019, while the men's Ballon d'Or has twice been decided by a single point.

That happened when England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton, who was later knighted, beat Portugal star Eusebio by the smallest possible margin in 1966, and Germany defender Matthias Sammer repeated the tight one-point victory when he edged out Brazil striker Ronaldo in 1996.

Mbappe may take heart from Ronaldo's Ballon d'Or experience as the legendary frontman, who presented Kane with his award in London on Monday, went on to win in 1997 and again in 2002.

Kane clinched the prize after scoring 73 goals in 65 matches last season, helping Bayern Munich to a league and cup double and leading England to a third-place finish at the World Cup.

The award is decided by votes from 100 journalists, using a weighted points system.

Top 10 in the 2026 men's Ballon d'Or:

  • Harry Kane - 1,055 points

  • Kylian Mbappe - 1,027 points

  • Lamine Yamal - 881 points

  • Rodri - 726 points

  • Lionel Messi - 612 points

  • Khvicha Kvaratskhelia - 541 points

  • Ousmane Dembele - 418 points

  • Erling Haaland - 378 points

  • Michael Olise - 296 points

  • Fabian Ruiz - 201 points

item.title: Parsons hat-trick as Irish seal South Africa series win
item.description: Beibhinn Parsons scores a hat-trick of tries as Ireland close out their WXV Global Series campaign by securing back-to-back wins over South Africa in Cape Town.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

WXV Global Series

South Africa (10) 17

Tries: Tose, Solontsi, Ubisi Con: Cilliers

Ireland (14) 38

Tries: King, Parsons 3, Dalton 2 Cons: O'Brien 4

Beibhinn Parsons scored a hat-trick of tries as Ireland closed out their WXV Global Series campaign by securing a historic Test series win over South Africa in Cape Town.

Winger Parsons, the team's all-time leading try-scorer, crossed once in the first half and twice after half-time to lift the Irish to a hard-fought win having fallen behind with 20 minutes left.

Captain Erin King and Aoife Dalton (2) also scored to help Ireland see off the Springboks in another bruising encounter at Athlone Stadium.

Unam Tose, Sizophila Solontsi and Vainah Ubisi crossed for the hosts, who were unable to avenge last week's 40-27 loss at the same venue.

In following up last week's win with another six-try display, Scott Bemand's side become the first Irish side to win back-to-back Tests on South African soil.

item.title: Hirakawa replaces Ocon for Mexico City Grand Prix
item.description: Ryo Hirakawa will race for Haas at the Mexico City Grand Prix, replacing Esteban Ocon.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Esteban Ocon has been replaced at Haas by the team's Japanese reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa for the remainder of the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Ocon, who is leaving the team at the end of the year, drove in Friday practice but the team released a statement on Saturday saying Hirakawa would drive instead of the Frenchman on Saturday and Sunday.

The team gave no further details about the reasons behind the decision, although a spokesperson at Haas said it was not because the Frenchman was ill.

The move comes after Ocon had a dispute with his race engineer Laura Mueller during second practice on Friday about tyre strategy.

Mueller told him over the radio that they were switching him to use the medium tyres on his race-simulation run because team-mate Oliver Bearman's run on the soft was "not great".

After Ocon asked for clarity, Mueller told him: "We have to do medium."

Ocon replied: "No, no. I wanted the soft. Don't do that to me. Come on."

Haas declined to comment on whether the decision to replace Ocon was related to the exchange and whatever aftermath it might have had.

Ocon is currently looking for a race seat for next year and it appears his chances are slim.

Only Cadillac and Racing Bulls have theoretical openings, but neither are said to be interested in him.

Hirakawa, 32, will be making his grand prix debut in Mexico. He is a two-time winner of the World Endurance Championship with Toyota, which is Haas' technical partner and title sponsor.

Hirakawa also drove in first practice on Friday in Mexico in Ocon's car.

Ocon is being replaced next year at Haas by Brazilian rookie Rafael Camara, a member of the Ferrari development driver programme.

item.title: Ulster undone by five-try Stormers in Cape Town
item.description: Ulster's search for an opening win in this season's United Rugby Championship [URC] goes on as they fall to a 33-7 defeat by the Stormers in Cape Town.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

United Rugby Championship

Stormers (12) 33

Tries: Schickerling, De Villiers, Roos, R Nel, Ahmed Cons: Ahmed 4

Ulster (7) 7

Tries: McCann Con: Murphy

Ulster's search for an opening win in this season's United Rugby Championship [URC] goes on as they fell to a 33-7 defeat by the Stormers in Cape Town.

Richie Murphy's side have now played five domestic fixtures which have produced three defeats and two draws.

Following last week's defeat by the Bulls in Pretoria, Ulster went into this second game of the South Africa tour without their Ireland contingent, who reported back before November's Nations Championship fixtures.

It left them with some gaps to plug, but they would perform admirably for much of this contest as David McCann powered over for the opening score.

However, quickfire tries before the break gave the hosts the lead and a third from Evan Roos minutes into the second period left them in a hole they never really looked like getting out of.

It is a fourth win from five URC fixtures for the Stormers, but far from a perfect display with plenty of unforced errors, yet they produced more than enough to prevail.

Ulster will now have to wait until they visit Cardiff on 5 December for their next opportunity to grab an opening league win.

Stormers strike either side of the break

In an error-strewn opening half, handling errors would halt Stormers' momentum on a number of occasions and eventually see them punished midway through the opening half.

McCann pounced on a knock-on to get his side on the front foot and although the TMO ruled out a score for Matthew Devine from the subsequent attack, play came back for an offside in the build-up and it was McCann who bundled over with Murphy converting.

A knock-on at the line by Cormac Izuchukwu saw Ulster spurn a glorious opportunity to grab a second just minutes later as momentum flipped with Ulster conceding four-straight penalties - the last of those resulting in Keynan Knox sent to the bin.

Pressure would eventually tell as JD Schickerling powered over and Ahmed added the extras before Paul de Villiers charged down Murphy's attempted clearance and took advantage to touch down to give Stormers a 12-7 advantage at the half.

Ulster were on the front foot early in the second period, but a blind pass by Devine was gleefully gathered by Roos, who put on the afterburners and galloped away for a converted score.

It left Murphy's side with a mountain to climb in the Cape Town heat as they could not make their presence felt in the opposite 22, the game played mostly in their own half as both sides continued to make errors.

However, it would finally stick for the hosts as a perfectly-weighted crossfield kick by Ahmed was fielded by team captain Ruhan Nel, who touched down for the bonus point.

Izuchukwu was denied a consolation score when held up over the line which summed up Ulster's day as the hosts finished with a flourish, Ahmed crossing for a fifth he would convert.

It put a seal on the win for the hosts, with Ulster now left with much to ponder as the first block of URC games comes to a conclusion.

While they continue to produce moments, Murphy's side are yet to find a fully-rounded display to get their season fully on track.

Stormers: Willemse; Senatla, R Nel (capt), Muller, Zas; Ahmed, Reinach; Mchunu, Paulo, Louw, Smith, Schickerling, De Villiers, L Nel, Roos.

Replacements: Rabe, Matongo, Fouché, Norton, Evans, Mlaba, Pead, Simelane.

Ulster: McIlroy; Lowry, Hume, Carson, Ward; Murphy, Devine; O'Sullivan, Herring, Knox, Donnell, Snyman, Izuchukwu, McCann (capt), Augustus.

Replacements: Walker, McAllister, Wilson, Sheridan, Moloney, McKee, Flannery, Mullins.

Referee: Sam Grove-White

item.title: A 3/10 that might be generous - player ratings for Chelsea v Man Utd
item.description: Player ratings as Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer score second-half goals in Chelsea's home win over Manchester United, who have Lisandro Martinez sent off.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer scored second-half goals as Chelsea secured a 2-0 home win over 10-man Manchester United, who endured another desperate day.

Chelsea's record £117m signing Rogers opened the scoring in the 50th minute before United defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off after conceding a penalty, which Palmer converted.

Here's how BBC Sport's reporters at Stamford Bridge rated the players and your verdicts on the performances.

Chelsea

Mike Penders: The Belgian goalkeeper remains under pressure after his mistake against Tottenham last week, but he was steady here and made several comfortable saves. 7

Josh Acheampong: The young defender looked shaky early on but recovered well, making a fantastic block from a Bruno Fernandes volley and improving as the game went on. 6

Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman made a brilliant block from one of Amad Diallo's shots but was twice at fault as the winger broke clear on the counter-attack. His header also struck the post after taking a deflection off Moises Caicedo in a chaotic display. Fofana also won the second-half penalty. 5

Levi Colwill: The England defender was part of an overall poor defensive display but did not make any obvious errors himself. 6

Marco Palestra: The Italian made some good recovery runs on his first start for Chelsea but was also part of a below-par defensive display from an organisational perspective. 7

Moises Caicedo: Influential presence in a scrappy midfield battle, helping Chelsea compete physically in the centre of the pitch. 6

Romeo Lavia: Often the player who helped Chelsea play through United's pressure, sparking several counter-attacks with intelligent passing. Won the ball for Chelsea's opener. 7

Pedro Neto: Arguably Chelsea's most dangerous attacker but finishing let him down, with one effort saved and another fired well wide in the first half. 6

Cole Palmer: A quiet game by his standards and unconvincingly scored a second-half penalty. Aside from that, he attempted an ambitious effort from inside his own half and gifted United one of their major chances. 6

Estevao Willian: Lost possession with his first touch but recovered impressively. Looked lively throughout, having a couple of dangerous-looking shots on goal and two that he scored but were ruled out for offside. His set-pieces were also of consistent high quality. 8

Morgan Rogers: A surprisingly anonymous start and struggled in the number nine position until he was given the chance to run at United's defence, scoring with a sublime dink in the 50th minute. 8

Subs:

Pep Chavarria (on 71, Palestra): Game was already won when he entered. 6

Malo Gusto (on 86, Pedro Neto)

Valentin Barco (on 86, Estevao Willian)

Danny Welbeck (on 86, Moises Caicedo)

Geovany Quenda on 90, Cole Palmer)

Manchester United

Senne Lammens: Alive to Palmer's attempt to catch him out with a quickly taken free-kick. Was lucky to get away with a poor save early on, thanks to offside flag. Solid after that. No chance with Rogers goal. 7

Leny Yoro: Speed essential to deal with Chelsea counter-attacks but sometimes ran out of position. 7

Harry Maguire: Authoritative presence at heart of defence for most part but yet again unable to stop gap opening up for Rogers to score. 7

Lisandro Martinez: Did OK and looked good - until Chelsea scored. Then gave penalty away and red-carded for ridiculous moment of recklessness. 3

Diogo Dalot: Played out of position again at left-back and Estevao threatened down his side, but Dalot stuck to his task gamely. 6

Andrey Santos: So close to a memorable goal against his old club. Crucial intervention to deny Moises Caicedo a clear sight at goal at the other end. Difficult second half. 5

Carlos Baleba: Was having his best game in a United shirt so far and tried to prod the visitors forward. But impetuous tackle in midfield proved extremely costly as Rogers ran through to score. 5

Amad Diallo: Looked sharp. Tested Mike Penders from long range and also at his near post. Fofana blocked another goal-bound effort. Should have scored before half-time. 7

Bruno Fernandes: Returned as captain and should have put the visitors ahead when Mbeumo picked him out. Nearly set up Mbeumo. Better but not brilliant. 6

Matheus Cunha: Most impact of any recent game. Linked well with the visitors' attack but didn't threaten a goal. 6

Bryan Mbeumo: Set up a chance for Fernandes, then nearly reached a far-post cross from his captain. Gave Chelsea a problem but couldn't get last bit right. 6

Subs:

Kobbie Mainoo (on 58, Baleba): Not on long enough to make an impact before Martinez red. After that it was damage limitation. 6

Ayden Heaven (on 66, Andrey Santos): Time for a regular start? 5

Mason Mount (on 66, Cunha): Usual abuse from the home fans and nothing to answer it with. 5

Joshua Zirkzee (on 77, Amad): 5

How did you rate the players?

Player of the match

After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.

item.title: Carragher apologises to Villa for 'wrong' language
item.description: Jamie Carragher apologises for "clumsy and wrong" language when linking manager Unai Emery with becoming Manchester United head coach, after Aston Villa threatened to sue him.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Jamie Carragher has apologised to Aston Villa, the club's owners and their fans for using "clumsy and wrong" language when linking manager Unai Emery with becoming Manchester United head coach.

On Friday, Villa said they would initiate legal action against the former England defender for what they described as "unacceptable insults".

The club's statement, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, referred to comments made by Carragher on the Stick to Football podcast, when he suggested Emery would want to manage a "giant" club.

He also told the club's fans to shut up, adding: "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

Posting on social media on Saturday, Carragher said his comments were intended to be "tongue in cheek".

"I'd like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans," the pundit wrote.

"My language this week was clumsy and wrong.

"I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it's not come across that way, so apologies."

Manchester United manager Michael Carrick's position is hanging in the balance following a dismal start to the season.

Referring to former Paris St-Germain and Arsenal boss Emery, Carragher said on Stick to Football: "Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again.

"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

After his comments attracted criticism from Villa fans, Carragher responded on social media, stating that telling them to shut up had been "a joke" and he had been praising Emery and the club "for years".

He reiterated on the Overlap Daily podcast that his message to Villa fans had been meant "in jest", adding: "I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking, what's the best we can get?"

item.title: 'Un-Australian' - Warner tears into former side after SA charge to win
item.description: Australia crumble under the pressure of a final-day chase as South Africa charge to a famous Test and series victory.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Third Test, Cape Town (day five of five)

South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101

Australia 429 & 111: Lyon 33*; Rabada 3-39; Harmer 6-16

South Africa won by 176 runs

David Warner labelled Australia "terrible", "utterly disgraceful" and "un-Australian" as his former side crumbled under the pressure of a final-day chase and allowed South Africa to charge to a famous Test and series victory in Cape Town.

Chasing 288 to win an enthralling contest themselves, Australia lost two wickets in the first over bowled by Kagiso Rabada and never recovered.

Rabada was irresistible, also adding the key wicket of Travis Head caught at slip in a superb first spell to become the fastest bowler to 350 Test wickets.

But Australia played a part in their own downfall, with Josh Inglis run out for four after inexplicably being called through by Cameron Green.

That opened the door to spinner Simon Harmer, who had Alex Carey caught reverse sweeping with just two to his name and Cooper Connolly caught behind for a two-ball duck.

At 60-7 at lunch, former opener Warner, who retired from Test cricket in January 2024, tore into his former team-mates.

"It is terrible," he said on Fox Sports. "It is un-Australian. There is no fight whatsoever. It is disgraceful.

"The batters have let the bowlers down all series. [Matt] Renshaw showed fight in that first Test but I think the batters have been utterly disgraceful."

Australia then dropped anchor in a bizarre period - one scoring shot came in 50 minutes - but Harmer was not to be denied, taking the final wicket for career-best figures of 6-16 as Australia were dismissed for 111.

Defeat comes at the start of an intense run of Test cricket for Pat Cummins' side, with attention now turning to four Tests at home against New Zealand starting in December before a five-Test tour of India, the 150th anniversary Test against England in March and next summer's Ashes. The consequences could be significant.

South Africa's fine victory, earned across three fascinatingly fluctuating Tests, means the Proteas regain their position at the top of the world rankings and reaffirms their status as one of the world's very best sides.

Un-Australian? How tourists collapsed to defeat

The series appeared in the balance before its 15th and final day. In the end, it was no contest. South Africa were sensational.

Warner's verdict came after the first session in which all Australian hope of victory had evaporated.

After opener Matt Renshaw was unfortunate to be caught down the leg side second ball, Marnus Labuschagne could not survive the remainder of the first over as he was dismissed shouldering arms. It extended the 32-year-old's run of innings without a century to 49. The 32-year-old's Test career looks to be over for now.

Without the determination of injured former captain Steve Smith, Australia's fresh-looking batting line-up, which did show promise in the first innings, appeared brittle.

At 40-3, they still had slim hopes but Green ran out Inglis and then Carey played his silly reverse off Harmer. Green, dropped on 10, survived to lunch but at one stage he was being protected from Harmer's spin by number eight Mitchell Starc.

"Yes, Matt Renshaw was burgled down the leg side, [but] it is on the line and this is the way they play," Warner said. "It is deplorable."

After lunch, and ironically given Warner's words, Australia changed tack completely, with Cummins facing 40 balls before scoring a run as he abandoned any thought of victory with two sessions to go.

When Green did face Harmer he was bowled through the gate.

That meant number 10 Nathan Lyon, who played his shots while Cummins blocked, finished as the innings' highest scorer with 33 not out.

item.title: New Zealand into semis with statement win over Fiji
item.description: New Zealand deliver a statement victory as they thrash Fiji 78-0 to book their place in the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

New Zealand delivered a statement victory as they thrashed Fiji 78-0 to book their place in the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.

The Kiwis established a 24-0 lead with four converted tries in the opening 13 minutes as Fiji - who pushed reigning champions Australia close a week ago - had no response on Australia's Gold Coast.

Fiji conceded eight tries in the first half and five in a fiery second period, during which half-back Brandon Wakeham was sent off along with New Zealand winger Ronaldo Mulitalo.

Centre Casey McLean claimed four tries, Keano Kini scored two and Jahrome Hughes, Dane Gagai, James Fisher-Harris, Mulitalo, Xavier Willison, Briton Nikora and Erin Clark also crossed for Stacey Jones' team.

"Pretty special and pleased about how we went about our business," said New Zealand captain Fisher-Harris.

"Fiji are a good team but I thought we played really well. It was a battle of the forwards."

Fiji's woes were not confined to the scoreline, with captain Apisai Koroisau suffering a suspected broken jaw as he clashed heads with Joseph Tapine in the eighth minute.

Semi Valemei, who impressed with a hat-trick of tries against the Kangaroos, also left the field with a head injury during the first half.

Meanwhile, New Zealand will now face an anxious wait to discover if Mulitalo faces a tournament-ending ban for a high shot on Ronald Philitoga, which prompted a fracas involving Wakeham.

However, in his post-match news conference Kiwis head coach Jones confirmed that star full-back Kalyn Ponga, who broke his arm in the tournament opener against Australia on 15 October, has trained this week and could be involved in their last-four match against either Samoa, Tonga or England.

Samoa and Tonga meet on Sunday and both look set to advance from Pool B & C.

England's slim hopes rest on the unlikely scenario of Tonga defeating Samoa by more than 46 points.

The losers of the contest between the Pacific Island rivals will take on Australia next.

Kevin Walters' side maintained their 100% record in their final group match with a comfortable 66-6 success over the Cook Islands in Townsville.

Jack Bostock and Tom Trbojevic both scored three tries each in a game the Cook Islands briefly led 6-4 when Rua Ngatikaura went over and Valentine Holmes added the extras.

Kiwi Ferns tune up for Samoa meeting

New Zealand women tuned up for their World Cup semi-final meeting with Samoa next Saturday with a 40-12 win over Papua New Guinea.

Mackenzie Wiki and Abigail Roache both scored two tries, while Stacey Waaka, Kaiyah Atai, Otesa Pule and Leianne Tufuga also added a try each.

Debutants Fiji will take on Australia in the other last-four match after registering 10 tries in a comprehensive 54-6 triumph over France.

In the wheelchair competition, captain Bayley McKenna starred with 44 points that comprised four tries and 14 goals from 15 attempts, as Australia demolished New Zealand 102-14 in Wollongong.

France, the runners up in 2022, opened their Pool B campaign with a thumping 114-0 win over Scotland.

Jeremy Bourson scored seven of France's 20 tries, while Jonathan Hivernat and Adrien Zittel registered another nine between them, with Scotland unable to offer any real resistance.

item.title: Lynn hails grit of 13-player Wales in Japan win
item.description: Wales head coach Sean Lynn has praised the grit shown by his side during their five-try victory over Japan.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Wales head coach Sean Lynn has praised the grit shown by his side during their five-try victory over Japan.

Wales looked comfortable in the WXV contest at 29-5 until replacements Keira Bevan and Hannah Dallavalle were yellow-carded within two minutes of each other.

It left them defending for their lives in the final 10 minutes in Kumagaya City with the hosts launching wave after wave of attack.

And while Japan carry the Brave Blossoms nickname, Wales were more than worthy of the tag themselves as they refused to concede.

"We knew it was going to be another tough one," said Lynn.

"The grit we showed to go down to 13 players and just hold them out at the end, that for me is just a sign of how far this squad has come.

"Everybody told me how amazing Japan is and for us to come away to win two Test matches is an amazing achievement from all players and staff. A huge pat on the back to everyone."

Lynn's post-match praise was echoed by co-captain Kate Williams.

Reflecting on the performance, she said: "We were brave with the ball and I think that showed in the tries that we scored. We can be really pleased with our set piece as well.

"Something that we need to continually work on is our discipline, but I'm really proud of the defensive effort, especially in that last 20 minutes with the two yellow cards."

The Welsh performance was far from perfect but it was another victory for a side which could not buy a win this time last year.

It also rounds off a successful WXV campaign, with Wales securing three wins from four in the Global Series and back-to-back Test wins for the first time in more than two years.

"We've got a really exciting team playing for Wales at the minute," said Williams.

"There's a really good mix of experience and young blood coming through and I'm really proud of all the girls who have stepped out onto the pitch, and also the girls who haven't made the 23, we've really galvanised as a group.

"We want to keep playing brave and keep reinforcing our DNA as Welsh players."

Wales travel back from Japan on Sunday before players head back to their Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) and Celtic Challenge clubs for the start of their domestic seasons.

Lynn said he will "stay connected" with the players before bringing them back into camp early next year for their Six Nations preparations.

Wales open their 2027 campaign at home to world champions England.

item.title: Briton Dart reaches first WTA Tour singles final
item.description: A tearful Harriet Dart said it "means the world" to her to qualify for her maiden WTA Tour singles final after battling past to beat China's Sun Xinran at the Guangzhou Open.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

A tearful Harriet Dart said it "means the world" to qualify for her maiden WTA Tour singles final after battling past Chinese wildcard Sun Xinran in three sets at the Guangzhou Open.

The 30-year-old qualifier recovered from failing to serve out the first set to save multiple match points in the second before closing out a 5-7 7-6 (6-1) 6-0 victory in a little under two and a half hours.

Dart, who made her WTA Tour debut in Eastbourne in 2015, was playing in just her second tour-level singles semi-final, having previously reached the last four at the 2024 Transylvania Open.

The British number five will face fourth seed Lilli Tagger or Kaitlin Quevedo in Sunday's final, knowing victory will secure her return to the top 100 in the WTA rankings. She has already climbed 14 places to 101st in the live standings.

"It's been a really long journey. I've wanted it so much, so badly - sometimes too much. To finally be here means the world," said Dart.

"I found it tough out there. It was a rollercoaster. Playing in this part of the competition, more nerves and more feelings come out. I was really battling with myself.

"I'm proud of the second set and was able to turn it quickly."

Trailing 3-0 in the first set after hitting a double fault on break point in her opening service game, Dart fought back to lead 5-4, dictating points from the baseline during a run of four consecutive service games.

She was visibly frustrated after hitting another two double faults as she served for the set.

Reigning US Open junior champion Sun, 16, made no such mistake, holding to 15 before breaking Dart for a third time to clinch the opener.

Dart twice had her nose in front in the second set, breaking Sun in the first and fifth games, but was immediately broken back on both occasions.

However, she held her nerve as she was twice required to serve to stay in the match before storming through the tie-break 7-1, silencing the crowd she had repeatedly complained to the chair umpire about in the process.

With her opponent struggling emotionally and physically, including receiving a medical timeout for treatment on her left leg, Dart cruised through the decider without dropping a game, winning 28 of the 41 points.

item.title: 'We fell behind' - what does new San Siro deal mean for AC Milan and Inter?
item.description: BBC Sport explores the plans for AC Milan and Inter's new stadium, and how powerful naming rights for new arenas can be
item.content:encoded:
• Published

When AC Milan and city rivals Inter jointly revealed the design of their planned new stadium on Thursday, one thing stood out in particular - the name.

The 71,500-seater arena the clubs aim to share from 2031 onwards, replacing the iconic San Siro, will be called the Generali Stadium.

Generali is an Italian insurance company, and the firm has agreed to pay about 650m euros (£542m) for naming rights through to 2052.

The length and value of the agreement makes it one of the most lucrative naming-rights deals in sports history.

Stadium naming rights are, of course, nothing new in elite football. The champions of England and Germany both play in arenas built in the 21st century that have always been known by their sponsors' name, and plenty more stadiums across the continent have been partly financed by revenue from naming rights.

But in recent years, some clubs have struggled to sell them.

It was thought that both Tottenham Hotspur and West Ham would look to sell the rights to their new stadiums' names, but as yet neither have. Liverpool aimed to sell the name of a new stand they built in 2016 but no such deal has been agreed.

So, what do these stadium plans mean for AC Milan and Inter, what underpins the viability of expensive new football grounds, and what impact do culture and history have?

Why do AC Milan and Inter want a new stadium with a sponsored name?

AC Milan and Inter are owned by separate US-based investment firms and in the joint announcement described the Generali Stadium as "a new home for generations of supporters, and a destination designed to contribute to the cultural, economic and urban development of the city".

The demolition of San Siro has been discussed for decades, and the clubs believe its deterioration and lack of modern features are significant reasons behind their progressive fall lower down the pecking order at the top of European football.

The new stadium is expected to cost about 1.2bn euros (£1bn) to construct, and the clubs aim to generate income by selling just under 12,000 of the seats as premium or hospitality, and host a wider array of events like concerts and fixtures in other sports.

"This is the biggest stadium naming-rights deal in the history of global sports," AC Milan owner Gerry Cardinale told BBC Sport.

"That’s a significant achievement in its own right and especially in the context of having been done in Italy and what it means to bring Italy back to the world stage of football.

"But if you’re looking at this purely as an annual sponsorship payment, you’re missing the bigger picture.

"The stadium is what fundamentally transforms our economic model - matchday revenues, hospitality, premium experiences, entertainment and commercial opportunities.

"These are the things that allow us to compete with the biggest clubs in Europe."

AC Milan have played at San Siro for 100 years, while Inter moved in 1947. The two clubs paid 197m euros (£164m) to buy the stadium and surrounding land in 2025.

The plans for the new stadium have faced opposition from some supporters, with some Inter fans protesting outside the venue where the plans were announced by carrying a banner reading 'You will never extinguish the lights at San Siro' and chanting "Hands off San Siro".

"You cannot compete consistently with the best clubs in the world without having the infrastructure and economic model to support that ambition," added Cardinale.

"The Premier League has set the benchmark in terms of commercial development and infrastructure. Italian football has fallen behind, and we need to change that.

"This stadium is a massive step forward, not just for AC Milan but potentially for the whole of Serie A."

Does the money make sense?

The two decades of naming rights paid for by Generali break down to about £27m per season - £13.5m per year, per club.

New stadiums are rarely built in Italy, with many Serie A stadiums in varying states of disrepair and in need of renovation before the country jointly hosts Euro 2032 with Turkey.

That means AC Milan and Inter have focused on selling a rare proposition.

"The 20-year deal is key - having that guaranteed long-term incomes gives the clubs security," said Dan Plumley - sport finance professor at Sheffield Hallam University.

"The money stacks up pretty well. Spotify pay around 20m euros (£17m) to sponsor Barcelona's Camp Nou per season, so now the Milan clubs aren't too far off that figure.

"What a lot of these partners are looking for is a long-term relationship because they can build their profile as expand around the world, pushing themselves into regions like Asia and Africa, and football can be very valuable for that.

"It couldn't be done at San Siro because everybody would have just carried on calling it that. Getting in early makes the sponsor part of the new history and is a really smart play from a business point of view."

What about stadium naming rights in England?

Historically, the home of stadium naming rights has been the US, where the majority of arenas in most sports are known by a sponsor name.

In European football, similar deals have been most common in Germany, where major companies have direct ownership links to some of the country's biggest clubs including Bayer Leverkusen and Wolfsburg.

"It's really difficult to do naming-rights deals in English football because of our history and culture," said Plumley.

"The clubs and potential naming partners know that fans around the world could strongly oppose a deal, because it's less common here, so the value becomes less attractive."

Timing and performance on the pitch are key considerations when clubs are planning to sell the stadium name.

"As a club you don't want to just do a cheap deal and give the name away for a few million just because it's extra revenue," said Plumley.

"Clubs like Spurs or West Ham know there is a trade-off between not just agreeing something because it's a bit of extra value, having a deal that genuinely makes a difference financially, and doing something that the fans will tolerate.

"Sometimes the balance just isn't right, and some of the most successful clubs in the world would rather hold on and protect their overall value and hold off and sell when their performance is at its peak - being in the Champions League is key to that.

"Everton weren't in a position in terms of results to go out and get a big global name paying a huge amount every year, so a more local partner [the Hill Dickinson law firm] made sense."

item.title: Listen: Shearer on MOTD, managerial jobs & scoring record
item.description: Kelly Somers speaks to former Premier League striker and pundit Alan Shearer.
item.content:encoded:
Episode details

Available for over a year

In this week’s edition of The Football Interview, Kelly Somers speaks to former Premier League striker and pundit Alan Shearer. They speak about his Premier League goalscoring record, leaving Newcastle for Southampton as a teenager and winning the Premier League with Blackburn Rovers. They discuss Alan Shearer the football fan and the feeling when Newcastle won the League Cup in 2025, their first trophy in his lifetime.
